body:
What natural-capital accounting records

Natural-capital accounting (NCA) systematically records environmental assets, changes in those assets and the flows of resources or ecosystem services associated with them. It organises environmental information so that changes can be compared across locations and accounting periods.

For example, a forest account may record how much forest exists, how its condition changes and which services it provides. A water account may record water resources, withdrawals and returns to the environment.

Accounting differs from a one-time valuation. A valuation may estimate the importance of a particular service on a particular date. An accounting system seeks consistent classifications, measurement boundaries and repeated observations over time.

System of Environmental-Economic Accounting

The System of Environmental-Economic Accounting (SEEA) is the United Nations framework for organising environmental and economic information in a consistent manner. It is designed to connect environmental data with the concepts used in the System of National Accounts (SNA).

SEEA Central Framework

The SEEA Central Framework (SEEA CF) was adopted by the United Nations Statistical Commission in 2012 as an international statistical standard.

It records relationships between the environment and the economy, including flows of energy, water and materials, environmental assets and changes in their stocks, emissions and waste, and relevant environmental economic activities.

SEEA Ecosystem Accounting

SEEA Ecosystem Accounting (SEEA EA) was adopted by the United Nations Statistical Commission in March 2021. It complements the Central Framework by examining ecosystems as assets, their condition and the services they supply.

The adoption has an important qualification: Chapters 1–7, covering the accounting framework and physical accounts, were adopted as an international statistical standard. Chapters 8–11, dealing with monetary valuation and integrated accounting, present internationally recognised statistical principles and recommendations.

The 5 core ecosystem accounts

AccountWhat it recordsExample
Ecosystem extentArea and changes in different ecosystem typesHectares of mangroves or wetlands
Ecosystem conditionCharacteristics indicating ecosystem quality or functioningVegetation condition or water quality
Physical ecosystem-service flowsServices supplied and used in physical unitsQuantity of an identified service supplied during a year
Monetary ecosystem-service flowsValues of identified service flowsAnnual monetary estimate of a service contribution
Monetary ecosystem assetsValue of ecosystem assets based on expected service flowsEstimated value of an ecosystem asset over its accounting life

Extent, condition and services answer different questions

The extent account asks how much ecosystem area exists. The condition account asks what state the ecosystem is in. Service-flow accounts ask what the ecosystem contributes during an accounting period.

A wetland may retain its extent while its condition deteriorates because of pollution. The quantity or quality of services it supplies may then decline. An extent account alone would not reveal the entire change.

Ecosystem accounts also have an important geographical dimension. Information can be organised for a country, state, river basin, coastal region or other defined area.

Physical accounting does not require monetary valuation. A reliable account of ecosystem area, condition or water use can be valuable for public decisions even when no monetary estimate is available.

Prelims focus

  • SEEA is the United Nations framework linking environmental and economic accounting.
  • The SEEA Central Framework was adopted as an international statistical standard in 2012.
  • SEEA Ecosystem Accounting was adopted in March 2021.
  • SEEA EA has 5 core accounts covering extent, condition, physical service flows, monetary service flows and monetary ecosystem assets.
  • SEEA EA Chapters 1–7 form the adopted international statistical standard; Chapters 8–11 provide internationally recognised principles and recommendations.
  • Trap: Natural-capital accounting is not restricted to assigning monetary values to ecosystems.

[References: United Nations, System of Environmental-Economic Accounting—Central Framework, introduction and framework overview, adopted 2012; United Nations, SEEA Ecosystem Accounting, introduction and five core accounts, adopted March 2021; United Nations SEEA, SEEA Implementation Guide, Introduction, sections on the 2012 and 2021 standards, consulted 1 November 2026.]

title: Natural-Capital Accounting and the SEEA Framework

body:
What GDP measures

Gross Domestic Product (GDP) measures the value of final goods and services produced within an economy's territory during a specified period. It is an important indicator of economic activity, but it is not designed to measure the complete condition of natural capital or every aspect of human well-being.

For example, extracting minerals can contribute to current production and GDP. At the same time, extraction reduces the remaining mineral stock. GDP by itself does not show that reduction as a separate measure of natural-capital depletion.

Similarly, a forest may provide flood regulation or other ecosystem services without generating a corresponding market transaction. Important environmental contributions may therefore remain insufficiently visible in conventional economic indicators.

Gross production and the loss of assets

The distinction between gross and net measures helps explain why asset depletion matters. Gross measures do not necessarily deduct the consumption of assets used in production. Under the 2008 System of National Accounts (SNA), Net Domestic Product (NDP) is GDP after deducting the consumption of fixed capital, such as the depreciation of produced assets.

However, NDP under the 2008 SNA does not automatically deduct every form of natural-resource depletion or ecosystem degradation. Under the 2025 SNA, NDP additionally deducts natural-resource depletion. Environmental-economic accounts provide additional information for assessing these changes.

A simple physical stock account

Illustrative renewable-resource account

Suppose a renewable resource begins a year with a stock of 100 units. During the year, natural regeneration adds 6 units and extraction removes 14 units.

Closing stock = 100 + 6 − 14 = 92 units.

The recorded stock has declined by 8 units. These are hypothetical physical quantities, not monetary estimates or official statistics.

The example shows why a record of extraction alone is insufficient. Sustainable use of a renewable resource depends partly on regeneration and other changes to the stock. For non-renewable mineral resources, extraction ordinarily reduces the remaining resource stock because comparable regeneration does not occur within normal human planning periods.

Environmentally adjusted indicators

Environmentally adjusted national accounts seek to make relevant natural-resource and environmental changes more visible alongside conventional economic aggregates.

The expression green GDP is commonly used for attempts to adjust economic output for selected environmental costs, such as resource depletion and degradation. It should not be confused with the SEEA itself. SEEA is a structured accounting framework; green GDP is a proposed or calculated adjusted indicator whose precise definition depends on the method used.

Therefore, a country can compile environmental accounts without automatically producing a single comprehensive official green-GDP figure.

Adjusted net savings

The World Bank's adjusted net savings (ANS), also known as genuine savings in some discussions, is a measure intended to provide information about changes affecting a country's long-term wealth.

Its published methodology begins with net national savings, adds education expenditure as a proxy for investment in human capital, and deducts selected natural-resource depletion and pollution damages.

In the World Bank indicator that includes particulate-emission damage, deductions include energy depletion, mineral depletion, net forest depletion, carbon dioxide emissions damage and particulate emissions damage.

A persistently negative adjusted-net-savings measure can signal that a country is failing to maintain the assets needed to support future well-being. However, the indicator is incomplete: some ecosystem degradation, resource losses and dimensions of human capital are difficult to measure and are not fully covered.

Keep the indicators separate

MeasureMain question answered
GDPHow much final economic output was produced?
Physical natural-capital accountHow did an environmental asset or resource stock change?
Monetary ecosystem accountWhat is the estimated monetary contribution or asset value under the accounting method?
Adjusted net savingsAre selected savings and asset changes consistent with building or maintaining long-term wealth?

These measures should be used together rather than treated as interchangeable. A rise in GDP does not, by itself, establish that natural capital has increased or that development is sustainable.

Prelims focus

  • GDP measures economic production, not the complete condition of natural capital.
  • Under the 2008 SNA, NDP deducts the consumption of fixed capital from GDP; the 2025 SNA additionally deducts natural-resource depletion.
  • Natural-resource depletion may occur alongside an increase in GDP.
  • Adjusted net savings includes selected adjustments for education expenditure, resource depletion and pollution damage.
  • SEEA is an accounting framework, whereas green GDP refers to an environmentally adjusted economic indicator.
  • Trap: Neither adjusted net savings nor green GDP captures every ecological and social cost.

[References: NCERT, Introductory Macroeconomics, Class 12 Economics, Chapter 2, National Income Accounting, conceptual definitions of GDP and NDP; World Bank, World Development Indicators, metadata for Adjusted Net Savings Including Particulate Emission Damage, indicator NY.ADJ.SVNG.GN.ZS, consulted 1 November 2026; United Nations SEEA, Frequently Asked Questions, relationship between SEEA and national accounts, consulted 1 November 2026.]

title: GDP, Environmental Depletion and Adjusted Economic Accounts

body:
India's institutions and initiatives

India's work on green skills and natural-capital accounting involves different institutions with different responsibilities. The Ministry of Environment, Forest and Climate Change (MoEFCC) is associated with environmental programmes and green skills, while the Ministry of Statistics and Programme Implementation (MoSPI) develops official environmental-economic statistical accounts.

Green Skill Development Programme

The Green Skill Development Programme (GSDP) was launched by MoEFCC in June 2017 as a pilot under the Environmental Information System (ENVIS) scheme. The pilot covered 10 locations in 9 biogeographic regions. The programme was extended to a wider national scale during 2018–19.

Its purpose was to develop practical skills that could support employment or self-employment in environment-related activities. Training areas included pollution monitoring, operation of sewage and effluent treatment plants, waste management, forest management and water-related conservation work.

These dates describe the documented launch and expansion of the programme. They should not be treated as proof of a particular number of active training centres or current trainees in 2026.

Environmental-economic accounts in India

MoSPI has undertaken environmental-economic accounting work using the United Nations SEEA framework since 2018. Its publications and studies cover subjects such as forests, minerals, water, wetlands, biodiversity, energy and ecosystem services.

On 25 September 2025, MoSPI released Environmental Accounting on Forest—2025, a dedicated publication covering national and state-level forest accounts. It includes information on forest assets, extent, condition and ecosystem services.

The publication brings together measurements from different data periods. For example, the associated official release discusses forest extent and condition changes over 2013–2023, while forest provisioning-service values cover 2011–12 to 2021–22. These historical measurement periods must not be confused with the 2025 publication date.

On 27 April 2026, MoSPI released EnviStats India: Frequently Asked Questions 2026 to explain environmental-economic accounting and related concepts, including forest accounts and pollination services.

On 7 October 2026, MoSPI released its Strategy for Environmental Economic Accounts in India 2026–2030. It sets out priorities for expanding environmental accounts, addressing information gaps and developing work on subjects such as forests, minerals, soil, water, carbon stocks and biodiversity.

The 2026–2030 strategy is a roadmap. Its publication does not establish that every proposed account has already been completed or that all environmental assets in India have been fully valued.

Gujarat's mangroves as natural capital

Mangroves in coastal Gujarat provide a useful example of the relationship between environmental assets, ecosystem services and livelihoods. Important mangrove areas occur around the Gulf of Kachchh and Gulf of Khambhat.

A healthy mangrove ecosystem can contribute to shoreline protection, fisheries, biodiversity conservation and climate resilience. It also supports livelihoods connected with coastal ecosystems.

For natural-capital accounting, the same mangrove area can be examined in several different ways:

  • Extent: The area occupied by mangrove ecosystems.
  • Condition: Indicators of vegetation health, ecosystem structure and ecological quality.
  • Physical service flows: Measurable contributions such as identified fisheries-related or coastal-protection services.
  • Monetary service flows: Carefully estimated values of selected services, where defensible methods and data are available.

These measurements are not interchangeable. Plantation activity does not automatically establish that the resulting mangrove ecosystem has survived, reached ecological maturity or restored every ecosystem service.

MISHTI and the Gujarat connection

The Mangrove Initiative for Shoreline Habitats and Tangible Incomes (MISHTI) combines mangrove restoration objectives with the protection of coastal habitats and livelihoods.

At an official workshop in Bhuj on 13 September 2026, MoEFCC reported that Gujarat had covered 27,652 hectares under MISHTI against a 2023–2027 target of 29,250 hectares. The reported coverage included 12,450 hectares in the Kori Creek region.

These figures represent the programme coverage reported on that date. They are not, by themselves, a measurement of long-term mangrove survival, ecosystem condition or monetary ecosystem-service value.

How green-economy policy and natural-capital accounting work together

Green-economy policies seek to change activities such as energy production, transport, industry, resource use and ecosystem management. These changes can create employment opportunities and also affect land, water, biodiversity and other environmental assets.

Natural-capital accounts provide evidence about the environmental assets and services affected by these choices. Green-job assessments provide evidence about the resulting work, skills and employment conditions. Together, they help evaluate whether economic changes are environmentally beneficial and socially inclusive.

Prelims focus

  • MoEFCC launched the Green Skill Development Programme in June 2017 under ENVIS.
  • The GSDP pilot covered 10 locations across 9 biogeographic regions; wider expansion followed in 2018–19.
  • MoSPI has undertaken SEEA-based environmental-economic accounting work since 2018.
  • Environmental Accounting on Forest—2025 was released on 25 September 2025.
  • MoSPI released its Strategy for Environmental Economic Accounts in India 2026–2030 on 7 October 2026.
  • As reported on 13 September 2026, Gujarat's MISHTI coverage was 27,652 hectares against a 2023–2027 target of 29,250 hectares.
  • Trap: Programme coverage, ecosystem extent, ecosystem condition and ecosystem-service value are different measurements.

[References: Ministry of Environment, Forest and Climate Change, PIB, Green Skill Development Programme, parliamentary reply, December 2021, programme launch and expansion; MoSPI, PIB, Environmental Accounting on Forest 2025, released 25 September 2025, physical asset, extent, condition and services accounts; MoSPI, PIB, EnviStats India: Frequently Asked Questions 2026, released 27 April 2026; MoSPI, PIB, Strategy for Environmental Economic Accounts in India 2026–2030, released 7 October 2026; MoEFCC, PIB, Workshop on Mangrove Conservation in Bhuj and MISHTI Progress, 13 September 2026; sources consulted 1 November 2026.]
